127.title: This one counts
127.hook: Epictetus: when you kiss your child, remember they are mortal (Discourses 3.24)
127.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism sometimes follow Epictetus's advice from the Discourses and the Handbook: in a moment of affection, they quietly remember that the one they love is mortal, and let it deepen their attention.

segments.voice: Yesterday: premeditatio, Seneca's rehearsal after a city burned. Your line was foreseen is lighter. Did you think once, calmly, it might not go this way, and then enjoy it when it did? Day one hundred twenty-seven.

It's bedtime. You lean over a sleeping child, or a partner, or an old dog curled on the rug, and for a second, out of nowhere, a thought arrives that you'd rather not have. One day, this won't be here. Most of us flinch from that thought. We push it away, as if thinking it might make it happen. Nearly two thousand years ago, Epictetus told his students to do something that shocked some of them. Don't push it away. Let it come, right in the middle of the tenderest moment. Today: this one counts.
screen: `LEANING OVER A SLEEPING CHILD.` → `ONE DAY, THIS WON'T BE HERE.` → `DON'T PUSH IT AWAY.`

segments.voice: In the Discourses, book three, Epictetus says, in paraphrase: when you kiss your child, what harm is there in whispering, tomorrow you may die? A student objects: that's ill-omened. You'll bring bad luck. And Epictetus answers: is it ill-omened to say the grain will be harvested? Or that leaves fall in autumn? It's simply naming something that belongs to nature. There's nothing unlucky in the truth. In the Handbook he says it more briefly: when you kiss your child, remember you are kissing a human being, a mortal, so that if they die, you won't be shattered. That's Epictetus's own reason, and it's worth being honest about it. He's thinking about steadiness: loving what you have without pretending you'll have it forever. Some readers find that cold. But many people who try the practice find something else inside it. The thought doesn't make them love less. It makes the moment sharper. You don't take the goodnight for granted. You look a little longer. You say the thing you were going to say tomorrow. That's the whole week, really. Marcus rose above the city and saw everyone at once. Voyager showed us one speck. The astronauts looked back. Memento mori, remember you will die. Seneca rehearsed the loss so it couldn't ambush him. And now Epictetus brings it all the way home, to one face, one hug, one ordinary evening. Not someday. This one. This one counts.
screen: `TOMORROW YOU MAY DIE.` · `THE GRAIN WILL BE HARVESTED.` · `YOU ARE KISSING A MORTAL.` · `THE MOMENT GETS SHARPER.` · then, large: `THIS ONE COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hug someone and mean it. For now, a rehearsal. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone you love, a person or an animal. Picture their face. Let the true thought come, gently: they are mortal, and so am I. Don't push it away. Notice what it does to how you see them. Then picture the next time you'll greet them, and how you'd like to hold that moment. After the bell, if they're near, go and do it. The bell holds the time.
This one counts. Remembering, in a tender moment, that the one you love is mortal, so you don't take the moment for granted. Today's word.
Your line: this one counts. Today, at one goodbye or one goodnight, slow down. Look a little longer. Hug a little longer. Say the thing you were saving for tomorrow. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

128.title: Five remembrances
128.hook: the Buddha's five: I will age, fall ill, die, be parted from what I love, and my actions are my own (Anguttara Nikaya 5.57)
128.howItsDone: In many Buddhist communities, especially in the Theravada and Plum Village traditions, the five remembrances are recited aloud, often daily, as part of a chanting session.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Epictetus said to remember, even while you kiss someone you love, that they are mortal. Your line was this one counts. Who did you hug? Day one hundred twenty-eight.

Most of us keep a little list in our heads of things we'd rather not think about. The dentist appointment. The email we haven't opened. And, much further down, the big ones: getting old, getting sick, the people we'll one day lose. We don't open that list on purpose. Now picture a teacher who asks people, every one of them, monks and parents and farmers alike, to take that list out and read it. Often. Slowly. Not to frighten themselves, but because, he says, it frees something. This whole week has been about keeping endings in view: the view from above, memento mori, Seneca's rehearsal, the hug that counts. Today the Buddha closes the week with his list. Today's practice is the five remembrances.
screen: `THE LIST WE DON'T OPEN.` → `READ IT OFTEN.` → `THE FIVE REMEMBRANCES.`

segments.voice: The list comes from a short teaching in the Anguttara Nikaya, the collection of the Buddha's numbered discourses, book of fives, number fifty-seven. Here they are, in plain words. One: I will grow old; I can't escape aging. Two: I will fall ill; I can't escape illness. Three: I will die; I can't escape death. Four: everything and everyone dear to me will change, and I will be parted from them. And five: my actions are my own. I am their owner and their heir; whatever I do, good or harmful, that is what I will inherit. The surprise is who it's for. The text says these should be reflected on often by women and men, by householders and by monks. Not just the monastery. Everyone. And it gives reasons. Remembering age softens the pride of youth. Remembering illness softens the pride of health. Remembering death softens the pride of simply being alive. Remembering parting loosens the grip of craving. And then the fifth turns everything around. The first four are about what will happen to you. The fifth is about what you do. Age, illness, death and parting are not up to you, and that sounds a lot like Epictetus two weeks ago, but here the Buddha adds something of his own: one thing you really do own is your conduct. So the list doesn't end in gloom. It ends in your hands. You can't stop the clock. You can choose what you say at dinner tonight.
screen: `FROM THE BOOK OF FIVES.` · `AGE, ILLNESS, DEATH, PARTING.` · `FOR EVERYONE, NOT JUST MONKS.` · `THE FIFTH: WHAT I DO.` · then, large: `MY ACTIONS ARE MY OWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read the five slowly. Settle, and let your breath find its own pace. Say each one inside, and give it a whole breath before the next. I will grow old. I will fall ill. I will die. I will be parted from what I love. My actions are my own. If one of them stings, let it. Notice the body, then soften the shoulders. Then stay with the fifth, and let it point at one thing you'll do today. The bell holds the time.
Five remembrances. Four things that will happen to everyone, and one thing that belongs to you: what you do. Today's word.

Your line: my actions are my own. Today, when something happens that you can't control, say the line and pick your next action on purpose. And tomorrow, we get up and walk. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

129.title: Solved by walking
129.hook: a Latin saying, later attached to Diogenes: it is solved by walking
129.howItsDone: Many writers, philosophers and ordinary people take a walk to think a problem through, and the Latin phrase solvitur ambulando is often quoted to describe it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the five remembrances, ending with the one thing you own. Your line was my actions are my own. What did you choose on purpose? Day one hundred twenty-nine.

You know the feeling. You've been staring at the same problem for an hour. The email you can't word. The decision about the job, the move, the conversation. You've made lists. You've asked three friends. Your head feels like a room with the windows shut. Then you give up, go for a walk to buy milk, and somewhere around the second corner the answer just, sort of, arrives. As if it was waiting for your legs. People have noticed this for a very long time, long enough to give it a Latin name. A new week starts today: walking, the body, and sleep. And it starts with three Latin words. Today's word is solvitur ambulando.
screen: `STUCK FOR AN HOUR.` → `A WALK FOR MILK.` → `THE ANSWER ARRIVES.`

segments.voice: Solvitur ambulando means it is solved by walking. The story it's attached to is older than the phrase. In ancient Greece, the philosopher Zeno of Elea built famous puzzles meant to show that motion is impossible: to cross a room, you must first cross half of it, and half of that half, forever, so how do you ever arrive? The story goes that when someone argued this to Diogenes the Cynic, he didn't answer. He stood up and walked around. Diogenes Laertius, a biographer writing centuries later, tells a version of it. The Latin tag came much later again, and people have pinned it on Diogenes ever since. So we can't say Diogenes ever spoke those words; the sources simply don't reach that far. But the idea caught on, and it grew. Philosophers took long walks to think. Nietzsche wrote that only thoughts that come from walking have any value. And modern science has poked at it too. In a 2014 Stanford study, people came up with more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, even walking on a treadmill facing a blank wall. It was a lab task, not a life decision, so it's a clue, not a promise. Still, notice what walking does. It moves the body, so the mind loosens its grip. It gives your eyes something new every few steps. And it sets a gentle rhythm, left, right, that your thoughts can ride on. Sometimes you don't solve it. You walk it.
screen: `IT IS SOLVED BY WALKING.` · `DIOGENES STANDS UP AND WALKS.` · `A LATIN TAG, ADDED LATER.` · `THE 2014 STANFORD WALKERS.` · then, large: `WALK IT OUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one question to walk with. Settle first. Let one question come up, something real you've been chewing on. Say it once, clearly, inside. Then set it down, the way you'd put a bag on the floor. Feel your feet. Picture your walk later today, ten minutes, the question riding along but not driving. For now, just breathe with it nearby. The bell holds the time.
Solvitur ambulando. Latin for it is solved by walking, a saying pinned on Diogenes, who answered an argument by getting up and moving. Today's word.
Your line: walk it out. Today, take a ten-minute walk with your one question. Don't force an answer; just let it walk beside you. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

130.title: Walking meditation
130.hook: slow walking, feeling each step, as taught in Buddhist monasteries
130.howItsDone: In many Buddhist monasteries, monks and visitors alternate sitting meditation with walking meditation on a short straight path, walking slowly and turning at each end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Diogenes stood up and walked, and the Latin said it is solved by walking. Your line was walk it out. Did your question walk with you? Day one hundred thirty.

Yesterday's walk was for thinking. Today's walk is for not thinking. Picture a monastery courtyard in Thailand or Myanmar, early morning. A monk walks a straight path of maybe twenty paces. At the end, he stops, turns slowly, and walks back. Then again. And again. For an hour. He isn't going anywhere, and that's the point. Most of our walking is getting from here to there: to the car, to the fridge, to the next thing, with the mind already arrived. This kind of walking has nowhere to arrive. Every step is the whole trip. Today's practice is walking meditation.
screen: `A MONK ON A SHORT PATH.` → `TURN, AND WALK BACK.` → `NOWHERE TO ARRIVE.`

segments.voice: In the Pali texts, the word for it is cankama, walking up and down, and the walking path itself carries the same name. Early Buddhist monasteries had paths built for it. And the Buddha, in one short teaching from the book of fives, lists five benefits of walking meditation. It gives you endurance for journeys. It gives you endurance for effort. It's good for health. It helps digestion. And the calm you find while walking lasts a long time. That last one matters: a calm that can walk is a calm you can take into the day. The practice looks different from school to school. In Burmese vipassana, taught by teachers like Mahasi Sayadaw, you break each step into parts and note them silently: lifting, moving, placing. In Zen, kinhin is walking meditation between long sits, slow, hands held at the chest, one half step to each breath. In the twentieth century, the Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh taught walking meditation to huge crowds, often outdoors, and made it one of the best-known Buddhist practices in the West. The common thread is simple. Feel the foot. Feel the weight shift. Let the next step be the only step. When your mind drifts to the grocery list, and it will, you notice, and come back to the sole of your foot. It's the same move as watching the breath, done with legs.
screen: `CANKAMA: WALKING UP AND DOWN.` · `FIVE BENEFITS OF WALKING.` · `LIFTING, MOVING, PLACING.` · `FEEL THE FOOT, COME BACK.` · then, large: `THIS STEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ten slow steps. If you can stand, stand. If not, do it with your feet on the floor where you sit. Shift your weight into one foot. Lift the other. Move it forward. Place it. Feel the heel, then the whole sole, take the weight. Say inside: this step. Then the next. Ten steps, slower than feels normal. If you run out of room, turn slowly and come back. The bell holds the time.
Walking meditation. Slow steps on a short path, feeling each one, taught in Buddhist monasteries for centuries. Today's word.
Your line: this step. Today, take the ten steps from one room to the next as a walking meditation. Feel the floor. Say your line once. Day one hundred thirty.

131.title: Thoreau's sauntering
131.hook: in his essay Walking (1862), Thoreau praises going out with no destination
131.howItsDone: Many people who love Thoreau take aimless walks in his spirit, without a route or a goal, and his essay Walking is still widely read by hikers and nature writers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, walking meditation: a short path, slow steps, turn and come back. Your line was this step. Did you feel the floor? Day one hundred thirty-one.

When did you last go out with no errand? Not to the store, not to hit a step count, not walking the dog on its schedule. Just out the door, turning left because left looked nice. For most of us, the honest answer is: a long time ago. Maybe as a kid. Now meet a man in Concord, Massachusetts, in the eighteen fifties, who did it for hours every single day, and thought it was one of the most serious things a person could do. He wrote an essay about it, printed in the year he died. Today's practice is Thoreau's sauntering.
screen: `NO ERRAND, NO STEP COUNT.` → `CONCORD, THE 1850S.` → `THOREAU'S SAUNTERING.`

segments.voice: Henry David Thoreau is best known for Walden, his two years in a cabin by a pond. But his essay Walking, published in the Atlantic in 1862, just after his death, may be the most fun thing he wrote. It opens boldly: "I wish to speak a word for Nature, for absolute freedom and wildness." Then he says he's met only one or two people in his life who understood the art of walking, people "who had a genius, so to speak, for sauntering." And he plays with where the word saunter comes from. One story, he says, is that it comes from wanderers in the Middle Ages who asked for charity on their way, they claimed, to the Holy Land, la Sainte Terre. So a saunterer is a Holy-Lander, and every walk can be a small pilgrimage. Another story he offers: sans terre, without land or home, and so at home everywhere. Here's the honest part. Modern dictionaries say nobody really knows where saunter comes from, and Thoreau's stories are almost certainly more poetry than history. He probably knew it. But look at what he's doing with them. He's saying a walk without a destination isn't lazy. It's a kind of pilgrimage, where the holy land is wherever your feet happen to be. He claimed he needed four hours a day of it to stay well in body and spirit. You don't need four hours. You need one walk where nothing is the goal.
screen: `WALKING, 1862.` · `A GENIUS FOR SAUNTERING.` · `HOLY-LANDER, OR WITHOUT LAND.` · `NOBODY KNOWS THE ROOT.` · then, large: `SAUNTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan a walk with no destination. Settle, and breathe. Picture your front door. Now picture stepping out and turning whichever way looks inviting. No errand, no route, no timer except maybe a rough sense of when to head home. Notice what that feels like in your body: freedom, or a little itch to be useful. Both are fine. Choose when today you'll go, even for ten minutes. The bell holds the time.
Thoreau's sauntering. Walking with no destination, which he treated as a small pilgrimage with the holy land wherever you are. Today's word.
Your line: saunter. Today, go out once with nowhere to be. Turn where it looks good. Come home when you feel like it. Day one hundred thirty-one.

132.title: The body scan
132.hook: moving attention from feet to head, central to Jon Kabat-Zinn's MBSR course (1979), drawn from Buddhist practice
132.howItsDone: In Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction courses, participants practice a guided body scan, usually lying down for about forty-five minutes, moving attention slowly through the body from the feet to the head.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thoreau and the art of going nowhere in particular. Your line was saunter. Where did your feet take you? Day one hundred thirty-two.

Quick question: how are your feet right now? You probably had to go and check. That's normal. Most of the day we live about six inches behind our eyes, and the rest of the body is something that carries the head around. It only gets our attention when it hurts. In 1979, in a hospital in Worcester, Massachusetts, a scientist named Jon Kabat-Zinn started a course for patients with chronic pain and illness that doctors had run out of ways to help. One of the first things he taught them was to lie down and visit their own bodies, one part at a time, starting at the toes. Today's practice is the body scan.
screen: `HOW ARE YOUR FEET?` → `A HOSPITAL, 1979.` → `THE BODY SCAN.`

segments.voice: The course was called Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction, MBSR for short, begun at the University of Massachusetts Medical Center. It's eight weeks long, and the body scan sits right at the start. You lie on your back and move your attention slowly: the toes of the left foot, the sole, the heel, the ankle, up the leg, then the right, the hips, the belly, the back, the hands, the arms, the shoulders, the neck, the face, the top of the head. At each place you simply notice. Warm, cold, tingling, aching, nothing at all. Nothing at all counts too. You're not trying to relax, though that often happens. You're trying to be there. Kabat-Zinn was open about where he learned this: from Buddhist meditation, which he practiced for years before shaping it for a hospital. And the roots go deep. In the Satipatthana Sutta, the Buddha's great teaching on mindfulness, one exercise is to review this very body from the soles of the feet up, and from the crown of the head down. The word in Pali is kayagatasati, mindfulness of the body. MBSR set the religious framing aside so anyone could use it, and it's been studied a great deal since, with real but moderate benefits for stress. Here's why it's worth five minutes. You spend all day living in your body. The scan is a way of showing up there on purpose, and saying, part by part: here I am.
screen: `MBSR: EIGHT WEEKS, 1979.` · `TOES TO THE TOP OF THE HEAD.` · `NOT RELAXING: BEING THERE.` · `ROOTS IN BUDDHIST PRACTICE.` · then, large: `HERE I AM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a short scan, feet to head. Sit or lie down. Start at your feet: what's there? Warmth, pressure, nothing. Move to the legs. The belly, rising and falling. The back against the chair or floor. The hands. The shoulders. The jaw. The eyes. The top of the head. Don't fix anything. Just visit. At the end, feel the whole body at once, and say inside: here I am. Later, if you can, try a slower one, five minutes. The bell holds the time.
The body scan. Attention moving slowly from the feet to the head, noticing without fixing, taught in MBSR and drawn from Buddhist practice. Today's word.
Your line: here I am. Today, once, scan feet to head for five minutes, lying down or sitting, and finish with your line. Day one hundred thirty-two.

133.title: Where you hold it
133.hook: stress often lands in the jaw, shoulders or belly
133.howItsDone: Many people use progressive muscle relaxation, tensing and then releasing each muscle group in turn, and relaxation courses often teach a quick check of the jaw, shoulders and belly during the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body scan, feet to head, noticing without fixing. Your line was here I am. What did you find on the way up? Day one hundred thirty-three.

Try this, right now, without changing anything first. Where are your shoulders? Are they sitting low and easy, or have they crept up toward your ears? And your teeth: touching, or pressed together? And your belly: soft, or pulled in like you're bracing for a hit? Most people who check find at least one of these on duty, holding something, for no reason they can name. That's what yesterday's scan was quietly turning up. Today we get specific. Today's practice is where you hold it.
screen: `SHOULDERS BY YOUR EARS?` → `TEETH PRESSED TOGETHER?` → `WHERE YOU HOLD IT.`

segments.voice: Here's what's going on. When the body senses a threat, it gets ready. In 1915 the American physiologist Walter Cannon gave that readiness a name that stuck: fight or flight. The heart speeds up, breathing quickens, and muscles tighten, ready to strike or run. That's useful if there's a bear. The trouble is that a hard email, a traffic jam or a tense dinner can set off a smaller version of the same thing, and there's nothing to strike and nowhere to run. So the tension just stays. And it tends to settle in the same few places. The jaw: many people clench their teeth when stressed, often without knowing, some even in their sleep. The shoulders: they rise and round forward, a little like a turtle pulling in. And the belly: the muscles brace, and breathing moves up into the chest. In 1929, a Chicago doctor named Edmund Jacobson published a book called Progressive Relaxation. His discovery was simple: people often can't feel how tense a muscle is until they first tighten it on purpose, and then let go. The contrast teaches the body what soft feels like. None of this needs a teacher or a mat. It needs a habit of checking. Your body is keeping score of the day in these three places. You can read the score, and you can put it down, one muscle at a time.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften the jaw, drop the shoulders. First the jaw. Let your teeth part a little, lips closed, tongue resting. Now the shoulders: lift them toward your ears on purpose, hold for a breath, and let them fall. Feel the difference. Do it once more. Then the belly: let it go soft, and let the breath drop down into it. Stay there, loose, and each time something tightens, notice, and let it down again. The bell holds the time.
Where you hold it. The jaw, the shoulders, the belly: the places the body stores a stressful day, and where you can set it down. Today's word.
Your line: let the shoulders down. Today, every time you open a message, check your shoulders and your jaw, and let them go. Day one hundred thirty-three.
